acronyms: Requests a service must handle each second; average = daily requests ÷ 86,400, design for the peak
The promised latency or availability; for a model service, the latency budget per request (e.g. p99 under 50 ms)
The time within which 99% of requests finish; the slowest 1% are what users notice
Average gap between predicted probability and observed rate across bins, weighted by how many rows fall in each bin
Ranking quality focused on the positive class; a random ranking scores the positive rate, so it's honest on rare positives
Square root of the average squared error, in the target's units; punishes big misses more than MAE
Clicks ÷ impressions; ad models predict it per impression.
Model log loss ÷ log loss of always predicting the base rate; 1.0 = no better than the base rate, lower is better.
An online optimizer for logistic regression with L1 sparsity and per-coordinate learning rates.
Boosted trees; at Facebook their leaf indices fed a logistic regression.

Predictions for each training row from the CV model that did not train on it

terms: Designing the whole system around a model: goal, metrics, labels, features, baseline, model, offline evaluation, A/B test, serving and monitoring
What the company cares about (fraud losses, retained revenue) vs what you can compute offline (recall at a budget, log loss); say how one maps to the other
A metric that must not get worse when you launch (complaints, latency, revenue elsewhere)
Quick arithmetic with round numbers (users × requests ÷ 86,400 × peak, rows × µs per row) to find the bottleneck before building
Batch precomputes predictions on a schedule into a table; online computes each prediction per request within a latency budget
Features computed differently (or at a different time) in production than in training, so offline scores don't hold; fix by logging served features and training on them
A data problem (a stale table, a feature going missing) that degrades predictions without any error; caught only by monitoring inputs and outcomes
Sculley et al.'s name for the maintenance cost of ML systems: glue code, feedback loops, entangled features (Changing Anything Changes Everything)
The smallest lift an A/B test is sized to detect; users per group ≈ 16·p(1−p)/δ² for 5% false alarms and 80% power
An interview assignment: a dataset, a question and a few hours; graded on framing, baseline, validation, error analysis and the write-up
What it is → why it works (with a number) → when it fails → what you'd do; a structure for any interview question
On rare positives a model that always says “no” is highly accurate and useless (99.83% on the credit-card fraud benchmark)
A short document shipped with a model: intended use, data, metrics, threshold, calibration, top features and limitations
Neural networks with many layers that learn their own features from raw inputs (pixels, audio, text); the default when no good columns exist
Block or act when p × cost of a miss > (1 − p) × cost of a false alarm, i.e. p > c<sub>FP</sub> ⁄ (c<sub>FP</sub> + c<sub>FN</sub>) for calibrated p.
A cardholder disputes a payment with their bank; the main (and late, up to ~120 days) fraud label.
Labels arrive long after the prediction, so recent data looks cleaner than it is; evaluate only on matured periods.
A count or sum over a recent time window (payments per card in the last hour), computed as of event time.
A feature from links between entities (cards per device or IP, shared addresses) that exposes fraud rings.
The period after the cutoff date in which the label is measured (e.g. churn in the next 30 days); features use only the observation window before the cutoff.
The predicted probability of the outcome (e.g. P(churn)), regardless of whether an action would change it.
How much an action changes the outcome for a person: P(outcome without) − P(outcome with); estimated from randomized tests.
persuadables / sure things / lost causes / sleeping dogs
The four kinds of customer by response to an offer; only persuadables are worth paying for, sleeping dogs react badly.
A combined feature such as ad × country, letting a linear model learn interactions.
Mapping feature strings into a fixed number of buckets with a hash; bounded memory at the cost of collisions.
Keeping all positives and a share w of negatives to cut training cost; recalibrate with q = p ⁄ (p + (1 − p) ⁄ w).
Average predicted probability ÷ observed rate; 1.0 is calibrated.
Kaggle scores submissions on one part of the hidden test set (public, visible during the contest) and re-ranks on the other part (private) at the end
The drop (or jump) in a submission's score and rank from the public to the private leaderboard; large when people chose by noisy public scores
Choosing models by many looks at the same holdout or leaderboard until its score is optimistic; selection picks luck
Blum & Hardt's demonstration: submit random labels, keep those above chance on the public LB, majority-vote them; the public score rises while the private stays at chance
Train a classifier to tell train rows from test rows; AUC ≈ 0.5 means they look alike, higher means drift, and its top features show what differs
checking whether CV can be trusted
Building the validation split the way the test differs from train (new customers → group split, future → time split)
Slicing validation errors by segment or feature range to see where a model fails and what to try next
Averaging the predicted probabilities of different models with weights tuned on out-of-fold predictions; helps when the models' errors differ
The simplest prediction (base rate, a simple rule or model) that every later idea must beat
A short document with problem, metric, validation design, baseline → final table, what failed, error analysis and risks
